scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm the asshole in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by laying out what's been happening. We've been dating for three years, and she's been struggling with her weight, gaining about 100 pounds since we started dating. I get that she has bipolar disorder, and I know from my own struggles with depression how food can be a coping mechanism. I don't want to come off as judgmental or unsupportive, especially since her mental health is already a sensitive area. But at the same time, I'm concerned about her health. I want her to feel good about herself and be healthy, and I think working on our diet together could be a positive way to approach this. I suggested that we both make changes together, so it doesn't feel like it's just her who needs to lose weight. I wanted to support her and make it a team effort, which I thought was a good approach. Last week, she decided to start working on her diet. But after just one week, she was upset because she hadn't lost any weight. I tried to encourage her by saying that it's too soon to see results and that she should focus on the long-term changes. But she was really defeatist, saying she'd never lose weight. That frustrated me because I felt like she wasn't fully committed, especially since she was still drinking soft drinks and eating chips, which are high in carbs. I brought up the idea that cutting out junk food completely might help her see quicker results. I didn't mean to criticize her, but just to offer a suggestion. But she got angry and told me to stop arguing with her about her weight. I tried to explain that I wasn't bringing up her weight, just discussing her diet and how her choices were affecting her progress. But she shut down and is now upset with me for hours. I understand that her bipolar disorder makes her sensitive to being challenged, and she tends to shut down when she feels criticized. But I'm wondering if I overstepped by challenging her defeatist attitude and pointing out her shortcuts with junk food. Am I being too pushy? Or is it reasonable to want to support her in making healthier choices? On one hand, I want to be supportive and understanding, especially considering her mental health challenges. I don't want to add to her stress or make her feel worse about herself. On the other hand, I do care about her health and well-being, and I want to help her in a way that's constructive. Maybe I should have approached the conversation differently. Instead of pointing out her junk food consumption, I could have focused on encouraging her and reinforcing the idea that progress takes time. I could have acknowledged her efforts and expressed confidence in her ability to succeed, rather than focusing on the setbacks. I also need to consider her feelings and how she perceives my involvement. She might feel like I'm criticizing her or not respecting her autonomy in making her own choices. It's important to respect her boundaries and let her take the lead in her own journey, even if I have suggestions or concerns. Perhaps I should have taken a step back and let her work through her feelings without adding my own frustration into the mix. I could have offered support in a way that doesn't involve direct criticism or suggestions, allowing her to feel more in control of her decisions. In the future, I should be more mindful of how I approach these conversations. Instead of focusing on what she's doing wrong, I can highlight the positive steps she's taking and express my belief in her ability to succeed. I can also be more patient and understanding, recognizing that change takes time and that setbacks are a natural part of the process. Overall, I think I need to strike a balance between being supportive and encouraging without overstepping or making her feel criticized. It's a delicate situation, especially considering her mental health challenges, and I want to ensure that I'm being the best partner I can be.
